keyPhrase: Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit
description: Understand the Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit and how it supports Atlantic R&D in our Canadian SR&ED glossary.

body.text: The Nova Scotia Research and Development Tax Credit is a 15% fully refundable provincial credit on eligible Nova Scotia R&D expenditures, with no upper expenditure limit. Administered by the Canada Revenue Agency alongside the federal SR&ED program, corporations claim it on Schedule 340 (Line 566 of Schedule 5) no later than 18 months after their tax year-end.

Canada operates one of the world's most comprehensive research and development (R&D) fiscal incentive frameworks, anchored federally by the Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Tax Incentive Program and complemented by an extensive network of provincial and territorial R&D tax credits and direct innovation grants1. Following the March 26, 2026 Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), Canada enacted the most substantial statutory expansion of the federal SR&ED program in over a decade, effective retroactively for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20241. Under the enacted legislation, the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced refundable Investment Tax Credit (ITC) doubled from $3.0 million to $6.0 million—increasing the maximum annual cash refund from $1.05 million to $2.1 million—while the taxable capital phase-out range widened from $10 million–$50 million to $15 million–$75 million1. Simultaneously, Parliament extended the 35% enhanced refundable rate to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) for the first time, introduced an elective three-year average gross revenue phase-out alternative for Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs), reinstated the eligibility of capital expenditures and equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024, and launched an optional Pre-Claim Approval process on April 1, 2026 that halves post-filing expenditure review timeframes from 180 calendar days to 90 calendar days1.

At the provincial level, the fiscal landscape underwent an equally transformative realignment in 2025 and 20268. Most notably, Québec eliminated eight legacy R&D tax credit measures for taxation years beginning after March 25, 2025, consolidating its innovation incentives into the new Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC), which provides a 30% refundable credit on the first $1.0 million of eligible R&D and pre-commercialization expenditures above an exclusion threshold (and 20% refundable thereafter), alongside the January 1, 2026 transition of its e-business tax credit (CDAE) into the artificial-intelligence-focused CDAEIA8. Saskatchewan also doubled its refundable R&D tax credit ceiling for CCPCs from $1.0 million to $2.0 million of qualifying expenditures for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, while British Columbia made its 10% SR&ED tax credit permanent and extended refundable eligibility to ECPCs9.
1. Legislative and Statutory Architecture of the Federal SR&ED Program
1.1 Dual-Mechanism Statutory Framework: Section 37 and Section 127 of the Income Tax Act

The federal SR&ED Tax Incentive Program is codified within the Canadian Income Tax Act (R.S.C., 1985, c. 1 (5th Supp.)) (the "ITA") and Part XXIX of the Income Tax Regulations (C.R.C., c. 945) (the "ITR")15. Rather than operating as a discretionary subsidy, the SR&ED program is a statutory entitlement structured around two distinct, sequential legal mechanisms that must be calculated separately on Form T661 (Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) Expenditures Claim) and Schedule T2SCH31 (Investment Tax Credit – Corporations) or Form T2038(IND) (Investment Tax Credit (Individuals))5.

The first mechanism is the Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures under Section 37 of the ITA. Under subsection 37(1) of the ITA, a taxpayer carrying on a business in Canada may deduct current and (for property acquired after December 15, 2024) capital expenditures incurred on SR&ED carried on in Canada directly by or on behalf of the taxpayer and related to a business of the taxpayer16. Unlike ordinary business expenses, which must be deducted in the taxation year incurred, allowable SR&ED expenditures enter a cumulative Section 37 expenditure pool21. A taxpayer may deduct all, part, or none of the positive balance in this pool in computing business income for the current taxation year, and any undeducted balance carries forward indefinitely to offset business income in future taxation years (subject to partnership restrictions and loss restriction event rules under subsection 37(6.1) and paragraph 37(1)(h))16. Separately, subsection 37(2) governs current expenditures on SR&ED carried on outside Canada: while foreign R&D expenses directly undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer remain currently deductible against business income under subsection 37(2), they do not enter the subsection 37(1) indefinite carryforward pool and do not generate an Investment Tax Credit, except to the limited extent that permissible direct employee salaries or wages qualify under the 10% foreign wage limit6.

The second mechanism is the SR&ED Investment Tax Credit under Sections 127 and 127.1 of the ITA. Once allowable expenditures are established under Section 37, subsections 127(5) to 127(12) and Section 127.1 govern the calculation, application, and refundability of Investment Tax Credits (ITCs) earned on the taxpayer's SR&ED qualified expenditure pool2. An expenditure can be deductible under Section 37 without generating an equivalent qualified expenditure under Section 127 (for example, non-arm's length SR&ED contract payments, or the 20% excluded portion of arm's length contract payments), and conversely, the notional Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) generates ITCs under Section 127 without ever entering the Section 37 deduction pool4.

body.text: 1.2 The 2024–2026 Legislative Transformation: 2024 Fall Economic Statement, Budget 2025, Bill C-15, and Budget 2026

Between December 2024 and November 2026, the federal SR&ED regime underwent a multi-stage legislative overhaul that reversed the restrictions imposed by the 2012 Federal Budget (which had eliminated capital expenditures and lease costs effective January 1, 2014, reduced the basic ITC rate from 20% to 15% after 2013, and lowered the PPA rate from 65% in 2012 and 60% in 2013 to 55% in 2014)4. Understanding the exact legislative sequence is vital for tax auditors and corporate claimants, because initial proposals announced in late 2024 were subsequently expanded before being enacted into law in March 20261:

items: The 2024 Fall Economic Statement (December 16, 2024) and August 2025 Draft Legislation: On December 16, 2024, the Department of Finance Canada tabled the 2024 Fall Economic Statement (FES), followed by detailed draft legislative amendments and explanatory notes in August 202516. The FES initially proposed four core reforms effective for taxation years beginning on or after December 16, 2024 (and property acquired on or after December 16, 2024): increasing the annual expenditure limit for the 35% enhanced ITC from $3.0 million to $4.5 million; expanding the prior-year taxable capital phase-out thresholds from $10M–$50M to $15M–$75M; extending the 35% enhanced refundable ITC to Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) subject to a $15M–$75M three-year average gross revenue phase-out (and allowing CCPCs to elect into the gross revenue phase-out formula); and fully reinstating the pre-2014 eligibility rules for capital expenditures and equipment lease costs6.

Federal Budget 2025 (November 4, 2025) and Royal Assent of Bill C-15 (March 26, 2026): On November 4, 2025, Minister of Finance and National Revenue François-Philippe Champagne presented Federal Budget 2025, which retained all the structural reforms of the 2024 FES but further increased the annual SR&ED expenditure limit from the proposed $4.5 million to $6.0 million, retroactive to taxation years beginning after December 15, 20241. These measures were codified in Bill C-15 (Budget 2025 Implementation Act, No. 1), which received Royal Assent on March 26, 20261. Consequently, any circulating guidance citing a $3.0 million or $4.5 million federal expenditure limit for post-December 15, 2024 taxation years is outdated; the legally enacted ceiling is $6.0 million, yielding up to $2.1 million in annual refundable ITCs at the 35% enhanced rate1.

CRA Operational Modernization (April 1, 2026): Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched the elective SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process (utilizing Form T1322) to provide upfront technical eligibility certainty within 8 weeks and reduce post-filing expenditure review processing times from 180 days to 90 days1. Concurrently, in May 2026, the CRA released updated versions of Form T661, Schedule T2SCH31, Schedule T2SCH49, Form T1145, and Form T1146 incorporating the restored capital property lines, pre-claim approval case numbers, and Canada Research and Development Classification (CRDC) codes5.

Federal Budget 2026 Innovation Measures: According to industry analysis of Federal Budget 2026, the government introduced the first targeted expansion of the SR&ED program toward commercialization activities to help Canadian enterprises convert R&D outputs into market-ready innovations, while allocating $298 million over three years to renew the Clean Technology initiative under the National Research Council of Canada's Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP), $1.0 billion over six years (starting in 2028–2029) to strengthen the Strategic Response Fund (formerly the Strategic Innovation Fund), and $181.4 million over four years to Invest in Canada46.

body.text: 1.3 Statutory Definition of SR&ED under Subsection 248(1) of the Income Tax Act

To qualify for either the Section 37 deduction or the Section 127 ITC, the underlying technical activities must satisfy the statutory definition of "scientific research and experimental development" in subsection 248(1) of the ITA22. Subsection 248(1) defines SR&ED as a systematic investigation or search that is carried out in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis and that falls within one of four positive categories, while explicitly excluding routine or commercial activities8.

Under the positive prongs of subsection 248(1), eligible work encompasses Basic Research under paragraph 248(1)(a), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge without a specific practical application in view, and Applied Research under paragraph 248(1)(b), defined as work undertaken for the advancement of scientific knowledge with a specific practical application in view8. The vast majority of industrial claims fall under Experimental Development in paragraph 248(1)(c), which comprises work undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement for the purpose of creating new, or improving existing, materials, devices, products, or processes, including incremental improvements thereto8. In addition, paragraph 248(1)(d) includes Support Work—specifically work undertaken by or on behalf of the taxpayer with respect to engineering, design, operations research, mathematical analysis, computer programming, data collection, testing, or psychological research, where the work is commensurate with the needs, and directly in support, of basic research, applied research, or experimental development described in paragraph (a), (b), or (c) that is undertaken in Canada by or on behalf of the taxpayer23. Support work never qualifies as SR&ED on a standalone basis; its eligibility is strictly derivative of eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development24. Furthermore, activities performed by tradespeople (such as electricians, welders, or mechanics) that do not fall within the eight enumerated support activities in paragraph (d) cannot be claimed as SR&ED support work under a contract, though they may qualify as directly related and incremental overhead under the Traditional Method24.

Conversely, subsection 248(1) writes explicit exclusions directly into the definition of SR&ED22. Even if an activity involves technical difficulty, it is legally barred from SR&ED eligibility (unless it forms part of the eight enumerated support activities commensurate with and directly supporting eligible work) if it is work with respect to: market research or sales promotion; quality control or routine testing of materials, devices, products, or processes; research in the social sciences or the humanities (a frequent audit disallowance area for data analytics firms); prospecting, exploring, or drilling for, or producing, minerals, petroleum, or natural gas; the commercial production of a new or improved material, device, or product or the commercial use of a new or improved process; style changes; or routine data collection22.
1.4 CRA Eligibility Guidelines: The "Why" and "How" Framework

In its administrative publication Guidelines on the eligibility of work for scientific research and experimental development (SR&ED) tax incentives, the CRA distils the statutory text of subsection 248(1) and the common-law principles of Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen into a two-stage analytical methodology known as the "Why" and "How" Requirements31.

The "Why" Requirement evaluates the scientific or technological purpose of the project: the claimant must demonstrate why the work was conducted—specifically, that it was undertaken for the purpose of advancing scientific knowledge or achieving a technological advancement by resolving an underlying scientific or technological uncertainty22. A technological uncertainty exists when whether a given result or objective can be achieved, or how to achieve it, is not known or cannot be determined on the basis of generally available scientific or technological knowledge or experience (the existing "knowledge base")31. Overcoming a complex technical problem using standard practice, vendor documentation, known engineering formulas, or routine debugging does not constitute resolving a technological uncertainty22. Similarly, in 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen (2021 TCC 17), the Tax Court of Canada clarified that while business constraints and economic considerations provide relevant context for framing a project, purely economic or cost-efficiency uncertainties do not qualify unless they manifest as genuine technological obstacles54. As emphasized in the CRA's Guide T4088 (Guide to Form T661), achieving commercial novelty, innovation, uniqueness, feature enhancement, or increased functionality in a product or software application does not, in itself, establish technological advancement5. Rather, the work must generate new information or knowledge that advances the business's understanding of scientific relations or technology to a higher level beyond the baseline that existed at the onset of the project5. Crucially, commercial or technical failure does not disqualify a claim: gaining an understanding of why a hypothesized solution will not succeed or meet desired objectives constitutes an eligible technological advancement because the rigorous rejection of a hypothesis eliminates a possible solution and advances the technological knowledge base31.

Once the "Why" requirement is satisfied, the "How" Requirement evaluates whether the work was carried out through a systematic investigation or search in a field of science or technology by means of experiment or analysis performed by qualified individuals31. The CRA guidelines define a systematic investigation through four mandatory operational elements:

items: Defining the Problem and Completing Due Diligence: Identifying the existing scientific or technological knowledge base and its specific limitations by reviewing scientific literature, technical publications, patents, industry standards, or prior trials43.

Formulating a Hypothesis: Generating an explicit hypothesis—an idea consistent with known facts that serves as a starting point for further investigation toward achieving an objective or resolving a problem51.

Testing by Experiment or Analysis: Methodically testing the idea or hypothesis through structured experimentation or analysis, observing and measuring results, and allowing the hypothesis to evolve and change as a result of testing51.

Developing Logical Conclusions and Keeping Contemporaneous Evidence: Formulating logical conclusions based on the results or findings of the experiment or analysis, and keeping evidence that is generated as the work progresses51.

body.text: 2. Federal SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Rates, Thresholds, and Refundability Rules
2.1 Enhanced 35% Rate vs. Basic 15% Rate

Under subsection 127(9) (paragraph (a.1) of the definition of "investment tax credit") and subsection 127(10.1) of the ITA, the federal SR&ED program operates a two-tier ITC rate structure2. The Enhanced 35% Rate consists of the 15% basic ITC rate under paragraph 127(9)(a.1) plus an additional 20% ITC enhancement under subsection 127(10.1), yielding a combined 35% ITC on qualified SR&ED expenditures up to the corporation's annual expenditure limit (maximum $6,000,000 for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; $3,000,000 for prior taxation years)2. The Basic 15% Rate applies to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by a CCPC or ECPC in excess of its annual expenditure limit, as well as to all qualified SR&ED expenditures incurred by foreign-controlled corporations, non-qualifying public corporations, individuals (sole proprietors), trusts, and partnerships1. When a claimant repays government assistance, non-government assistance, or a contract payment that previously reduced its qualified expenditures in an earlier taxation year, the ITC earned on the repayment is determined at the rate (35% or 15%) at which the ITC would have been earned in the taxation year the assistance or contract payment was originally received2.
2.2 Claimant Categories: CCPCs, ECPCs, and Other Entities
A claimant's entitlement to the 35% enhanced rate and cash refundability under Section 127.1 depends on its precise legal classification throughout the taxation year2.
Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations (CCPCs) are defined in subsection 125(7) of the ITA2. For refundability purposes under subsection 127.1(2), CCPCs are subdivided into three categories2:

items: Qualifying Corporation (Non-Excluded): A CCPC throughout a taxation year whose taxable income in the previous taxation year (or, if associated, the combined taxable income of the associated group) does not exceed its qualifying income limit2. Under subsection 127.1(2), the base qualifying income limit is $500,000, which is reduced when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated corporations passes $15 million (for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024; previously $10 million)2.

Excluded Corporation: Defined in subsection 127.1(2) of the ITA; an excluded CCPC receives a reduced 40% refundability rate on both current and capital expenditures up to and over the expenditure limit2.

Other CCPC (Other than Qualifying or Excluded): A CCPC whose prior-year taxable income exceeded its qualifying income limit (so it is not a "qualifying corporation"), but which still has a positive expenditure limit because its prior-year taxable capital (or 3-year average gross revenue, if elected) is below $75 million2.

body.text: Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) were added by Bill C-15 under subsection 127(9) for taxation years beginning after December 15, 20242. To qualify as an ECPC, a corporation must satisfy three statutory conditions throughout the taxation year: it must be resident in Canada; it must have a class of shares listed on a designated stock exchange (or, if not listed, have elected or been designated by the Minister of National Revenue to be a public corporation); and it must not be controlled by one or more non-resident persons27. In addition, under paragraph (b) of the eligible subsidiary definition in subsection 127(9), a Canadian-resident subsidiary corporation qualifies if not less than 90% ("all or substantially all") of the issued shares of each class of its capital stock are owned, directly or indirectly, by one or more corporations that are ECPCs27.

Foreign-Controlled and Other Corporations that are neither CCPCs nor ECPCs earn the 15% non-refundable basic ITC on all qualified SR&ED expenditures2. Individuals (sole proprietors) and certain trusts earn the 15% basic ITC, of which 40% is refundable in cash under Section 127.12. Partnerships do not pay income tax directly and cannot carry forward a Section 37 expenditure pool to a subsequent taxation year21. Instead, under subsection 96(1) and subsection 127(8), the partnership's pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures at the end of the fiscal year must be fully deducted in calculating the partnership's net income for tax purposes in that year, and the 15% ITC earned at the partnership level is allocated to active members (excluding "specified members" under subsection 248(1)), limited by each partner's "at-risk amount"2. Furthermore, under section 4.5 of the CRA's SR&ED Claims for Partnerships Policy, a partner cannot be an employee of the partnership; any salary or wages paid to a partner are treated as a distribution of partnership income and cannot be claimed as an SR&ED salary or wages expenditure58.
2.3 Annual Expenditure Limit ($6 Million) and Phase-Out Mechanics

For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, the maximum annual expenditure limit under subsection 127(10.2) (for CCPCs) and subsection 127(10.6) (for ECPCs) is $6,000,0002. This $6,000,000 limit is phased out on a straight-line basis between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000 based on either prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada or three-year average annual gross revenue2.

Under the Default Taxable Capital Phase-Out Method for CCPCs, unless a CCPC files an election to use the gross revenue method, its expenditure limit for a taxation year beginning after December 15, 2024 begins to decrease when the taxable capital employed in Canada (defined in the ITA, with reference to archived Interpretation Bulletin IT-532, Part I.3 – Tax on Large Corporations) of the CCPC and all associated CCPCs for the previous taxation year reaches $15,000,000, becoming nil ($0) when the previous year's taxable capital reaches $75,000,0002. Expressed as a straight-line reduction over the $60,000,000 phase-out range ($75,000,000 minus $15,000,000), the expenditure limit is calculated as:
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($75,000,000 − Prior-Year Taxable Capital Employed in Canada) ÷ $60,000,000]

Equivalently, for every $10 of prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, the $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced by $12. (Under the pre-December 16, 2024 rules, the $3,000,000 expenditure limit phased out between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000 of taxable capital2.)

Under the Three-Year Average Gross Revenue Phase-Out Method (Mandatory for ECPCs, Elective for CCPCs), subsections 127(10.6) to 127(10.64) establish a consolidated group revenue test for ECPCs2. The $6,000,000 expenditure limit is shared among members of a consolidated group that prepare consolidated financial statements (defined in subsection 127(9) as financial statements in which the assets, liabilities, income, expenses, and cash flows of the members of a group are presented as those of a single economic entity)2. If an entity leaves or joins the group during the year, the average annual revenue used is that of the consolidated group as reflected in the consolidated financial statements for the year in question2. The $6,000,000 expenditure limit is reduced on a straight-line basis when the average annual gross revenue over the three preceding fiscal years (or over the actual one or two fiscal years if fewer than three exist) is between $15,000,000 and $75,000,000, becoming nil at $75,000,0002:
Expenditure Limit = $6,000,000 × [($75,000,000 − Average Annual Gross Revenue) ÷ $60,000,000]

Crucially, for taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, a CCPC may elect (using the prescribed form) to have its expenditure limit determined based on the same three-year average gross revenue phase-out structure as an ECPC instead of the taxable capital structure2. This election benefits companies that have high taxable capital or belong to a large associated group, but have low gross revenues6.

In addition, short taxation years and group allocations are governed by subsections 127(10.21) to 127(10.64)2. If a corporation has a short taxation year, its expenditure limit is prorated under subsection 127(10.5) by multiplying the limit by the number of days in the taxation year divided by 3652. Specific rules also apply under subsection 127(10.5) and paragraph 127(10.64)(a) if a CCPC or ECPC has more than one taxation year ending in the same calendar year and is associated (or in a consolidated group) in two or more of those taxation years with another CCPC or ECPC that has a taxation year ending in the same calendar year2. Associated CCPCs must file Schedule T2SCH49 (Agreement Among Associated Canadian-Controlled Private Corporations to Allocate the Expenditure Limit) under subsection 127(10.3), while consolidated ECPCs file an election under subsection 127(10.62); otherwise, each member's limit is nil under subsections 127(10.21) and 127(10.61), and if a group fails to file an agreement within 30 days of a request by the Minister of National Revenue, the Minister will allocate the expenditure limit among the group under subsections 127(10.4) and 127(10.63)16.
2.4 Comprehensive Refundability Matrix and Carryover Provisions

Under Section 127.1 of the ITA, whether an earned SR&ED ITC is paid out as a cash refund (to the extent it exceeds the claimant's federal Part I tax payable) depends on the claimant's entity classification, whether the expenditure is within or above the annual expenditure limit, and whether the expenditure is a current expenditure (including the PPA) or a capital expenditure2. While current expenditures and the PPA within the $6.0 million limit attract a 100% refund rate (yielding a 35% effective cash refund: 100% × 35% = 35%), restored capital expenditures within the $6.0 million limit attract a 40% refund rate under subsection 127.1(2) (yielding a 14% immediate cash refund: 40% × 35% = 14%, with the remaining 21% ITC available to offset Part I tax payable)2.

body.text: Any unused federal SR&ED ITCs may be carried back 3 taxation years (to reduce federal Part I tax payable in those previous years) or carried forward up to 20 taxation years under subsection 127(5)2. Furthermore, any federal SR&ED ITC applied to reduce tax or refunded in cash in a taxation year reduces the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the subsequent taxation year (reported on Line 435 of Form T661)21. If reductions cause the Section 37 pool balance to become negative, the negative amount is included in income under paragraph 12(1)(v) of the ITA (and amounts included in income in a previous taxation year under paragraph 12(1)(v) are subsequently added back to increase the Section 37 pool)21. By contrast, provincial and territorial R&D tax credits constitute "government assistance" and reduce both the Section 37 pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool in the current taxation year21.
3. Qualifying SR&ED Expenditures (QREs) and Calculation Methodologies
3.1 Traditional Method vs. Proxy Method: Strategic Election and Mechanics

To compute allowable SR&ED expenditures and qualified expenditures on Form T661, every claimant must select one of two statutory accounting methods for each taxation year: the Proxy Method (elected by ticking Line 160 in Part 3 of Form T661, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(B) of the ITA and subsection 2900(4) of the ITR) or the Traditional Method (chosen by ticking Line 162 in Part 3 of Form T661, governed by clause 37(8)(a)(ii)(A) of the ITA)4. This selection is made on a year-by-year basis: a claimant is not locked into the method chosen in prior years, but once Form T661 is filed for a specific taxation year, the choice of method for that taxation year is irrevocable and cannot be changed5.

Under the Proxy Method, the claimant does not specifically identify, track, or allocate individual SR&ED overhead and other expenditures31. Instead, the claimant calculates a notional amount—the Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA)—equal to 55% of the salary base of employees directly engaged in SR&ED in Canada (calculated in Part 5, Section B, Line 820 of Form T661 and entered on Line 502 of Part 4)4. (Under subsection 2900(4) of the ITR, the PPA rate was 65% for 2012 and prior years, 60% for 2013, and has been 55% since 20144.)

The PPA is included exclusively in qualified SR&ED expenditures in Part 4 of Form T661 to earn Investment Tax Credits under Section 127; it is not included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures (Line 360 must be entered as "0"), and the actual overhead expenses represented by the PPA are deducted as regular business expenses4. Specifically, the PPA covers and replaces: office supplies; heat, water, electricity, and telephones; salary or wages for support staff; salary or wages of employees directly undertaking, supervising, or supporting SR&ED that are directly related but not directly engaged (such as long-term planning for future SR&ED projects or contract administration); non-SR&ED contract costs (such as electricians, welders, and mechanics) that are directly related and incremental to performing SR&ED; the employer's share of related benefits; travel and training; property taxes; maintenance and upkeep of SR&ED premises, facilities, or equipment; and any other eligible expenditure directly related and incremental to SR&ED31. Additionally, the PPA is subject to an overall cap in Part 5 of Form T661 ensuring that the sum of the PPA, other qualified SR&ED expenditures, and deductions allowed under other sections of the ITA (such as interest, Capital Cost Allowance, the Section 37 SR&ED deduction claimed on Line 411 of Schedule T2SCH1, and building rent) does not exceed total business expenses deducted for income tax purposes in the taxation year4.

Under the Traditional Method, the claimant enters "0" for the PPA on Line 502 (leaving Part 5 blank) and instead specifically identifies, tracks, and allocates all actual overhead and other expenditures incurred for SR&ED during the taxation year on Line 360 of Form T66131. Under the Traditional Method, eligible overhead expenditures are included in the Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures and also earn Section 127 ITCs (unless they are prescribed expenditures under Regulation 2902), provided the claimant can substantiate with cost records that each overhead item was directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada31.

body.text: 3.2 Salaries and Wages: Directly Engaged, Specified Employees, and Foreign R&D

Employee compensation is governed by subsection 248(1), subsection 37(9.1), Regulation 2900, and the CRA's SR&ED Salary or Wages Policy4. Under subsection 248(1) of the ITA, "salary or wages" means income of a taxpayer from an office or employment as computed under subdivision a of Division B of Part I of the ITA23. Eligible inclusions comprise basic salary or wages, vacation pay, statutory holiday pay, sick leave pay, pay in lieu of termination notice, tips and gratuities, honorariums, director's fees, management fees, commissions, inducements and non-competition payments, bonuses and remuneration based on profits for employees other than specified employees, and taxable benefits (such as automobile benefits, housing/board/meals, gifts and awards, interest-free or low-interest loans, group term life insurance policies, and tuition fees)23. Cash outlays for taxable benefits qualify directly, while non-cash taxable benefits qualify only if the value is a reasonable estimate of actual costs, excludes GST/HST or PST (unless no input tax credit can be claimed), and the actual costs are not claimed elsewhere as a business expense23.

Conversely, SR&ED salary or wages never include: the employer's share of related benefits (CPP/QPP, EI, WSIB/CNESST, approved employee pension or superannuation plans, medical/dental/optical insurance plans, supplementary sick benefits, or employee savings plans); salary or wages for extended vacation or sick leave (in excess of normal annual leave earned); stock option benefits; retiring allowances; dividends (which are not employment salary or wages); or any salary or wages not paid within 180 days of the end of the taxation year5.

Eligibility of an employee's salary depends on the actual tasks performed rather than job title23. Under the Proxy Method, only "directly engaged" (hands-on) duties under paragraphs 248(1)(a) to (d) qualify on Lines 300 and 305: conducting experimentation and analysis; performing support work commensurate with the needs and directly in support of SR&ED (including tasks by non-specialized employees supervised by staff with scientific or technological qualifications, such as operating a machine required for an experiment or feeding raw materials into a machine); first-line supervision directing the technical course of ongoing SR&ED or providing direct technical input; and technological planning for ongoing SR&ED projects claimed in the year (assigning technological personnel, job priorities, technological strategies, and material quality)23. Work beyond the first-line level of supervision, non-technological management, and clerical or administrative services (accounting, payroll, legal, human resources, purchasing, sales, shipping, inventory control, maintenance, and word processing) are not directly engaged23. Under the Traditional Method, administrative and clerical wages may be claimed on Line 360 as overhead only if they are directly related and incremental to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada23.

A specified employee is defined in subsection 248(1) of the ITA as an employee who does not deal at arm's length with the employer or who is a specified shareholder—meaning a person who owns, directly or indirectly at any time in the year (counting shares of non-arm's length persons), 10% or more of the issued shares of any class of the corporation or a related corporation26. Specified employees are subject to three strict statutory restrictions4:

items: Exclusion of Bonuses and Profit-Based Remuneration: Bonuses and remuneration based on profits paid to specified employees are completely excluded from allowable SR&ED salary or wages (Line 305) and from the PPA salary base (Line 816)4.

Maximum Allowable SR&ED Salary Cap — 5× YMPE (Subsection 37(9.1)): The maximum SR&ED salary or wages claimable on Line 305 for a specified employee is limited to 5 times the Year's Maximum Pensionable Earnings (YMPE) determined under section 18 of the Canada Pension Plan for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year on which the individual is a specified employee23. For the 2026 taxation year, the CPP YMPE is $74,600 (with a Year's Basic Exemption of $3,500 and a 5.95% CPP contribution rate outside Québec), resulting in a maximum allowable SR&ED salary cap of $373,000 (5 × $74,600) per specified employee for a full 365-day year26. Associated corporations must allocate this limit using Form T1174 (Agreement Between Associated Corporations to Allocate Salary or Wages of Specified Employees for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED))20.

Maximum PPA Salary Base Cap — Lesser of 75% of Total Salary or 2.5× YMPE (Regulation 2900(7)): Under subsection 2900(7) of the ITR, the maximum amount a claimant can include in the PPA salary base on Line 816 for a specified employee is restricted to the lesser of: (a) the directly engaged SR&ED salary claimed on Lines 305 and 309; (b) 75% of the specified employee's total salary or wages (both SR&ED and non-SR&ED, excluding bonuses, remuneration based on profits, taxable benefits, and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year); or (c) 2.5 times the YMPE for the calendar year in which the taxation year ends, prorated by the number of days in the taxation year that the claimant employed the individual (with no proration for time during the year that the employee was not a specified employee): 2.5 × YMPE × (Days Employed ÷ 365)4. For the 2026 taxation year (YMPE = $74,600), the 2.5× YMPE proxy salary base ceiling is $186,500 per specified employee (shared across associated corporations, including deemed associated individuals and partnerships)4. Furthermore, under subsection 2900(9) of the ITR, for all employees (both regular and specified), the PPA salary base must exclude taxable benefits, bonuses, remuneration based on profits, related benefits (employer contributions), and prior-year unpaid wages paid in the current year (Line 310)4.

body.text: In addition, claimants may claim permissible salary or wages for SR&ED work carried on outside Canada (reported on Line 265, Line 307 for non-specified employees, and Line 309 for specified employees on Form T661) if the work is directly undertaken by employees of the claimant and forms an integral part of the SR&ED carried on inside Canada by the claimant6. The permissible foreign salary or wages are limited to 10% of the total SR&ED salary or wages directly attributable to SR&ED carried on in Canada, are deemed incurred in Canada, and are included in the PPA salary base4.
3.3 Materials Consumed and Materials Transformed

Under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i) and the CRA's Materials for SR&ED Policy, the cost of raw materials, substances, or other physical and tangible items (in solid, liquid, or gaseous state) that compose the body of a tangible object on which SR&ED is carried out—or that results from SR&ED—can be claimed as a current expenditure (100% deductible and 100% eligible for ITCs) under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods in the taxation year in which the material is actually consumed or transformed in the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (not when purchased or removed from inventory)31.

Materials Consumed (Line 320 of Form T661) are items destroyed, rendered virtually valueless, or disposed of as waste during SR&ED testing (for example, cardboard boxes used to test a new printing process that have no residual or resale value after testing)31. Energy sources and process water integrated directly into a chemical or physical conversion reaction where the reaction is integral to or the subject of SR&ED also qualify as materials consumed62. Conversely, the CRA explicitly excludes broken or used lab supplies, cleaning supplies, general utilities (water, electricity, oil, natural gas), CDs/DVDs, and used lubricants such as engine oil from materials consumed62. Materials Transformed (Line 325 of Form T661) are component parts or materials incorporated into a custom product, commercial asset, experimental production, or prototype during SR&ED (for example, a new engine that is the subject of SR&ED incorporated into a commercial machine)31. If materials transformed into a property are subsequently sold or converted to commercial use within 20 years, the ITC earned on those materials is subject to ITC Recapture under subsections 127(27) to 127(36)34.
3.4 Contract Expenditures (Arm's Length vs. Non-Arm's Length) and Third-Party Payments

When a claimant contracts an arm's length party to perform SR&ED on its behalf in Canada (reported on Line 340 of Form T661), 100% of the allowable SR&ED contract expenditure enters the Section 37 deductible pool under subparagraph 37(1)(a)(i.01), but under subparagraph (a)(ii) of the definition of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9), only 80% of the allowable contract expenditure qualifies to earn an Investment Tax Credit under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods22. The work must be performed in Canada by a taxable supplier; if a contract covers both SR&ED and non-SR&ED work, the payment must be allocated (such as by fair market value) so that only the SR&ED portion is claimed24. While the payer earns the ITC on 80% of the contract, the arm's length contractor must deduct the "contract payment" received from its own SR&ED expenditures to prevent a double benefit24. Notably, if an arm's length contractor is contracted only to perform one of the eight enumerated support work activities in paragraph 248(1)(d), the contractor cannot claim SR&ED itself (as support work alone is not SR&ED), but the payer can claim the contract expenditure (at 80% for ITCs) provided the support work is commensurate with the needs and directly in support of the payer's eligible basic research, applied research, or experimental development24.

When a claimant enters into an SR&ED contract with a non-arm's length (NAL) performer (Section 251), 100% of the contract expenditure is an allowable Section 37 deduction for the payer (Line 345), but it is excluded from the payer's qualified expenditures for ITC purposes under paragraph (f) of "qualified expenditure" in subsection 127(9) and subsection 127(24) (deducted on Line 541 of Form T661)24. Instead, the NAL performer claims its own underlying SR&ED expenditures and ITCs directly (including support-work-only contracts under section 7.4 of the CRA policy), and the amount received from the NAL payer is not considered a "contract payment" and does not reduce the NAL performer's qualified expenditures24. Alternatively, under subsection 127(13), the NAL performer and NAL payer may file Form T1146 (Agreement to Transfer Qualified Expenditures Incurred in Respect of SR&ED Contracts Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length) to transfer qualified expenditures (including the PPA, up to the performer's net qualified expenditure pool) from the performer (Line 540) to the payer20. Where a claimant purchases goods or non-SR&ED services from a NAL supplier for SR&ED, subsection 127(11.6) caps the qualified expenditure at the NAL supplier's cost (Line 542 of Form T661)31.

Under subparagraphs 37(1)(a)(i.1) to (iii) and the CRA's Third-Party Payments Policy, a claimant may also claim third-party payments (Line 370 of Form T661, accompanied by Form T1263, Third-Party Payments for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED), for each payment) made to six categories of entities (Entities A through F) to be used for SR&ED carried on in Canada related to a business of the claimant, provided the claimant is entitled to exploit the results of the SR&ED27. Only 80% of a third-party payment qualifies for an ITC30. Eligible recipients are: A Entities (corporations resident in Canada, where incentives are earned in the year the SR&ED is performed, subject to prepaid expense rules in paragraphs 18(9)(a) and (d)); B Entities (approved associations); C Entities (approved universities, colleges, research institutes, or similar institutions); D Entities (non-profit SR&ED corporations resident in Canada and exempt from tax under paragraph 149(1)(j)); E Entities (approved granting councils that make payments to B, C, or D entities); and F Entities (non-profit SR&ED corporations exempt under paragraph 149(1)(j) conducting broadly based, precompetitive basic or applied consortium research in Canada whose results will be used in conjunction with the corporate claimant's own SR&ED)30. Payments in kind are valued at fair market value, and third-party payments cannot be used to acquire a building, leasehold interest in a building, or building rental expense under paragraph 37(8)(d)30.

body.text: 3.5 Overhead and Other Expenditures: Software, Cloud Computing, and Prescribed Exclusions

When a claimant uses the Traditional Method (Line 162), current expenditures claimed on Line 360 must be either directly attributable to the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (paragraph 2900(2)(c) of the ITR) or directly attributable to the provision of premises, facilities, or equipment for the prosecution of SR&ED in Canada (subsection 2900(3) of the ITR)31. Under the CRA's SR&ED Overhead and Other Expenditures Policy, an expenditure (or reasonable allocated portion) satisfies the "directly attributable" standard only if it meets two mandatory tests36:

items: The Directly Related Test: The expenditure must connect directly—with no intervening step or intermediary—to (i) the SR&ED work, (ii) the SR&ED staff, or (iii) the machinery or equipment used by staff to perform SR&ED36. For example, salaries of clerical/administrative staff directly supporting SR&ED work and incremental to it are allowable on Line 360, whereas related benefits, retiring allowances, training costs, and travel expenses for those same clerical/administrative staff are disallowed because there is an indirect link to the SR&ED work36.

The Incremental Test: The expenditure would not have been incurred had such prosecution of SR&ED not occurred36. Fixed monthly payments for telephone, cellular phones, or internet connectivity fail the incremental test because they would be incurred regardless of SR&ED, whereas long-distance telephone charges and identifiable incremental utility costs qualify31. Fixed-cost maintenance contracts and post-project waste disposal costs (incurred after the SR&ED activity has finished) also fail the incremental test36. Among personnel recruitment expenses, moving expenses for selected SR&ED candidates or relocating SR&ED employees between Canadian facilities qualify on Line 360 if directly related and incremental, whereas headhunter fees, job advertising expenses, interview travel costs, and immigration/work permit costs are deductible only as regular business expenses36.

body.text: Under Section 2902 of the ITR, "prescribed expenditures" are strictly excluded from "qualified expenditures" under subsection 127(9) and never earn Investment Tax Credits (even if deductible in the Section 37 pool under the Traditional Method)16. Prescribed expenditures include: general administration and management expenses (including administrative salaries and related benefits for personnel whose duties are not all or substantially all directed to SR&ED, unless directly attributable under the Regulations); legal or accounting fees (including patent applications and licensing agreements); fees for preparing SR&ED claims (financial or technical); interest and other financing costs under paragraphs 20(1)(c) to (g) of the ITA; entertainment expenses; advertising or selling expenses; conference or convention expenses; dues or membership fees in a scientific or technical society or organization; fines or penalties; and current maintenance/upkeep expenses not attributable to SR&ED35.
3.6 Reinstated Capital Expenditures, Shared-Use Equipment (SUE), and Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Bill C-15 reinstated SR&ED tax incentives for capital property acquired after December 15, 2024 and equipment lease costs first becoming payable after December 15, 20241. Capital expenditures or lease costs made before December 16, 2024 remain strictly ineligible2. The restored rules operate across three distinct categories:
1. SR&ED Capital Expenditures — All or Substantially All (ASA ≥ 90%) Test (Line 390)

Under paragraph 37(1)(b) and subsection 127(9) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA's SR&ED Capital Expenditures Policy (updated June 29, 2026), an expenditure to acquire depreciable property after December 15, 2024 qualifies as an SR&ED capital expenditure on Line 390 of Form T661 if it results in the claimant owning (or holding a leasehold interest in) property for which Capital Cost Allowance (CCA) could be claimed under paragraph 20(1)(a), and at the time of acquisition the claimant satisfies the ASA Intent Test—meaning the property is intended either to be used during all or substantially all (ASA, defined as 90% or more) of its operating time in its expected useful life in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada, or to have ASA (90% or more) of its value consumed in the prosecution of SR&ED carried on in Canada6. Evaluating the claimant's intent involves assessing the reason for purchase, potential and actual use, type of SR&ED, SR&ED environment, project length, past practices, and planning documents29.

Non-depreciable property (land, inventory, goodwill/eligible capital property), buildings, and leasehold interests in buildings (other than prescribed special-purpose buildings) are excluded under paragraph 37(8)(d)22. While used depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 that meets the 90% ASA test can be claimed on Line 390 for the Section 37 deduction pool, used equipment does not qualify for the Section 127 ITC (property must be new to earn the ITC)5. Capital cost includes the purchase price, installation costs, customs and excise duties, transportation, and other acquisition costs (entered on Line 390 and Box 782, with the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties per project listed on Lines 262 and 263 of Form T661)45. Under subsection 37(6), the Section 37 deduction for capital expenditures is deemed to be CCA allowed to the taxpayer; consequently, capital expenditures claimed on Line 390 must not be included on Schedule T2SCH8 (Capital Cost Allowance), and if not claimed on Form T661 by the 18-month reporting deadline, must instead be depreciated under standard CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH816.
2. Shared-Use Equipment (SUE) — Primarily (> 50% to < 90%) Test (Line 504)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Shared-Use-Equipment Policy (updated May 22, 2026) and subsection 127(9), new depreciable equipment acquired (available for use) after December 15, 2024 that does not meet the 90% ASA criterion because it is used for both SR&ED and commercial activities can qualify for partial ITCs on Line 504 (with the 20 most expensive SUE items listed in Part 6C of Form T661) under both the Traditional and Proxy Methods32. To qualify, the equipment must be brand new (not previously used, acquired for use, or rented for any purpose), must not be General Purpose Office Equipment or Furniture (GPOEF), and must not be Prescribed Depreciable Property (PDP) under subsection 2900(11) of the ITR (which excludes buildings, property intended for use in the assembly, construction, or commissioning of a commercial manufacturing/processing facility, plant, or line, and property intended at acquisition to be used primarily for non-SR&ED purposes)32.
Unlike the PDP test (which looks to intended use at acquisition), SUE eligibility depends on actual use during operating time32:

items: First Term SUE (25% Inclusion): Evaluates actual operating time during the First Period, which starts when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 12 months after that time32. If used primarily (more than 50% but less than 90%) for SR&ED in Canada during the First Period, 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost (excluding borrowing costs and adjusted for NAL transactions under subsection 127(11.6)) qualifies on Line 504 for an ITC32.

Second Term SUE (Additional 25% Inclusion): Evaluates actual operating time during the Second Period, which starts when the property becomes available for use and ends at the end of the first taxation year ending at least 24 months after that time32. Provided the property qualified as First Term SUE and is actually used primarily (> 50%) for SR&ED in Canada during the Second Period, the other 1/4 (25%) of the capital cost qualifies on Line 50432.

body.text: Because SUE is not part of the Section 37 pool, its capital cost is depreciated under regular CCA rules on Schedule T2SCH8 (where businesses also benefit from the 2024 FES reinstatement of the Accelerated Investment Incentive and Immediate Expensing for CCA Class 53 manufacturing/processing machinery, Class 43.1/43.2 clean energy equipment, and zero-emission vehicles acquired on or after January 1, 2025 and available for use before 2030), and any SUE ITC claimed or refunded reduces the Undepreciated Capital Cost (UCC) of the CCA class in the subsequent year32.
3. Equipment Lease Costs (Post-December 15, 2024)

Under the CRA's SR&ED Lease Expenditures Policy (updated June 8, 2026) and paragraph 37(1)(a) / subsection 37(8), lease expenditures incurred after December 15, 2024 for equipment used in SR&ED in Canada are allowable according to the claimant's chosen calculation method (evaluated over total operating time across the entire taxation year, or after December 15, 2024 for straddle years)28:

items: Under the Traditional Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(A)(I) and (II)): If leased equipment is used ASA (90% or more) of its operating time for SR&ED, 100% of the lease expenditure is claimable as a lease cost28. If used less than 90% of the time for SR&ED, the expenditure is claimable on Line 360 as overhead and other expenditures in the exact proportion of SR&ED operating time, provided it is directly related and incremental to SR&ED28. Lease costs for land incurred after December 15, 2024 are also claimable under the Traditional Method if ASA or directly attributable28.

Under the Proxy Method (Subclauses 37(8)(a)(ii)(B)(I) and (VI)): For leased premises, facilities, or equipment (excluding GPOEF and land), if SR&ED operating time is 90% or more (ASA), 100% of the lease cost is claimable; if SR&ED operating time is more than 50% but less than 90% (Primarily), 50% of the total lease cost is claimable; and if SR&ED operating time is 50% or less, 0% is claimable28.

Building Rent Prohibition: Under both methods, any expense to lease or use a building (rent) is strictly excluded, except for a prescribed special-purpose building approved by the Department of Finance Canada on a building-by-building basis (while non-building structures such as bridges or dams may qualify, and combined building-plus-equipment leases must be reasonably allocated)28.

body.text: 3.7 Unpaid Amounts (180-Day Rule) and ITC Recapture Mechanics

Under the 180-Day Unpaid Amounts Rules, employee salary or wages incurred in a taxation year but not paid within 180 days of the end of that taxation year (Line 315 of Form T661) are deemed not to have been incurred in that year and are excluded from both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and Section 127 qualified expenditures23. When paid in a subsequent year, they are claimed on Line 310 (entering the Section 37 pool and earning ITCs, but permanently excluded from the PPA salary base under Regulation 2900(9))4. Separately, under subsection 127(26) of the ITA, current expenditures other than salary or wages (such as materials, contracts, or overhead) that remain unpaid 180 days after year-end still enter the Section 37 deductible pool in the year incurred, but are excluded from Section 127 qualified expenditures until the subsequent taxation year in which they are paid (for an unpaid arm's length contract, 20% is first deducted under the 80% rule and the remaining 80% is deducted as an unpaid amount, with 80% added back in the later year when paid)35. Crucially, if an unpaid amount is not identified on Form T661 by the 18-month SR&ED reporting deadline for the year incurred, it can never be included in qualified expenditures even when paid in a later year35.

Under subsections 127(27) to 127(36) of the ITA and the CRA's Recapture of SR&ED Investment Tax Credit Policy, an ITC is recaptured (added to federal Part I tax payable) if all four conditions in subsection 127(27) are met: (1) the claimant acquired a particular property from a person or partnership in the current taxation year or in any of the 20 preceding taxation years (extended from 10 years to 20 years by subsection 127(36)); (2) the cost of the property was a qualified expenditure (materials transformed or incorporated into a commercial asset/product, ASA capital property, First or Second Term SUE, animals/growing things, or physical property acquired under an SR&ED contract); (3) a percentage of the property's cost was included in computing the claimant's ITC; and (4) in the current year, the claimant converts the property (or another property incorporating it) to commercial use, or disposes of it (for SUE, conversion occurs only when SR&ED usage becomes incidental, i.e., ASA converted to commercial use)24.

Recapture is calculated as the lesser of the ITC actually earned on the property and the applicable ITC rate multiplied by the proceeds of disposition (for arm's length sales) or Fair Market Value (FMV) (for commercial conversions or NAL sales)—multiplied by 25% or 50% in the case of First or Second Term SUE32. Under subsection 127(32), cost cannot exceed the amount paid to acquire the property from another person and excludes in-house salaries, wages, or overhead incurred to manufacture or modify a part in-house34. No recapture applies to the sale or licensing of Intellectual Property (IP), to scrap sales or low-FMV conversions where proceeds or FMV are less than 10% of the total cost of the property, to materials consumed unless insurance/recovery proceeds exceed 10% of cost, or to NAL dispositions of SR&ED capital property where the NAL purchaser continues to use the property as ASA capital property (subsections 127(34) and (35))24. Any ITC recaptured in a taxation year is added to increase the claimant's Section 37 pool of deductible SR&ED expenditures in the following taxation year21.
4. Interaction with Government Assistance, Grants, and Super-Allowances
4.1 Statutory Grinding Mechanics: Paragraph 37(1)(d) and Subsection 127(11.1)

Under paragraph 37(1)(d) and subsection 127(11.1) of the ITA, as detailed in the CRA's Assistance and Contract Payments Policy, both the Section 37 deductible expenditure pool and the Section 127 qualified expenditure pool (Lines 429 to 432 and Lines 513 to 517 of Form T661) must be reduced on a project-by-project basis by any government assistance, non-government assistance, or contract payments in respect of SR&ED that the claimant has received, is entitled to receive, or can reasonably be expected to receive on or before the filing-due date for the taxation year22.

Government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as assistance from a government, municipality, or other public authority (including Crown corporations, foreign governments, and non-profit entities funded by government organizations) whether as a grant, subsidy, forgivable loan, deduction from tax (including all provincial and territorial R&D tax credits), investment allowance, or any other form of assistance, excluding the federal SR&ED ITC itself27. Non-government assistance is defined in subsection 127(9) as an amount that would be included in income under paragraph 12(1)(x) (inducements, reimbursements, contributions, or allowances)33. If a government loan lacks firm repayment terms or has repayments conditional on future revenues or profits, or if—as held in CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King (2022 FCA 178)—a non-forgivable government loan carries a below-market implicit rate of return, the CRA and courts treat the contribution as government assistance that reduces SR&ED pools upon receipt33. Similarly, any provincial "super-allowance benefit amount" reduces the Section 37 and Section 127 pools under paragraph 127(9)(a.1)21. Where assistance exceeds a claimant's expenditures on a project performed jointly with a NAL party, subsections 127(19) and 127(20) govern the reduction and allocation of assistance using Form T1145 (Agreement to Allocate Assistance for SR&ED Between Persons Not Dealing at Arm's Length), and any subsequent repayment of assistance restores the Section 37 and Section 127 pools in the year repaid2.
4.2 Major Federal Innovation Funding Programs and SR&ED Stacking
Canadian claimants frequently combine direct federal innovation funding with SR&ED tax credits37. The primary federal grant and contribution programs interacting with SR&ED in 2026 are:

items: National Research Council of Canada Industrial Research Assistance Program (NRC IRAP): NRC IRAP provides non-repayable R&D contributions to Canadian SMEs (for-profit businesses incorporated in Canada with 500 or fewer full-time employees)65. Following the integration of Sustainable Development Technology Canada (SDTC) into NRC IRAP's Clean Technology (CTAS) stream—and the $298 million three-year renewal of NRC IRAP's Clean Technology initiative in Federal Budget 2026—engagement is mediated directly through an assigned NRC Industrial Technology Advisor (ITA)46. Once a formal proposal is submitted to an ITA, NRC IRAP's stated review timelines are 4 weeks for requests up to $50,000, 6 weeks for $50,000 to $500,000, 9 weeks for $500,000 to $3.0 million, and 13 weeks for $3.0 million to $10.0 million (following a 2-to-4-month ITA relationship and proposal-development phase)65. While the federal government announced in December 2023 that NRC IRAP would eventually be integrated into the new Canada Innovation Corporation (CIC) by 2026–2027, NRC IRAP remains the live delivery agency as of 202646. Crucially, under the Proxy Method, NRC IRAP salary grants do not reduce the Part 5 salary base used to calculate the 55% PPA; the 55% PPA is computed on the gross eligible SR&ED salary before deducting the IRAP assistance in Parts 3 and 44.

Strategic Response Fund (formerly Strategic Innovation Fund — SIF): Administered by Innovation, Science and Economic Development Canada (ISED) to support large-scale R&D, commercialization, and industrial transformation projects across all sectors (typically multi-stage applications taking 12 to 18+ months end-to-end)46. In Federal Budget 2026, the government proposed $1.0 billion over six years starting in 2028–2029 to strengthen the Strategic Response Fund46. Contributions received under this fund constitute government assistance under subsection 127(11.1)33.

body.text: 4.3 Worked Mathematical Examples: Federal-Provincial Stacking and Grant Grinding
To illustrate the exact statutory mechanics in force for the 2026 taxation year, consider three worked scenarios for a qualifying CCPC:
Scenario 1: CCPC Exceeding the New $6,000,000 Expenditure Limit ($8,000,000 Total QREs)

Consider a qualifying, non-excluded CCPC that incurs $8,000,000 in total qualified current SR&ED expenditures (including PPA) in its 2026 taxation year, with prior-year taxable capital below $15,000,000 and $0 Part I tax payable2:

items: First $6,000,000 at Enhanced 35% Rate: $6,000,000 × 35% = $2,100,000 (100% refundable under Section 127.1 = $2,100,000 cash refund)2.
Next $2,000,000 at Basic 15% Rate: $2,000,000 × 15% = $300,000 total basic ITC2.

40% Refundability on Excess for Qualifying CCPC: Because the claimant is a qualifying CCPC, 40% of the $300,000 basic ITC is refundable in cash: $300,000 × 40% = $120,000 cash refund, leaving $180,000 as a non-refundable ITC carryforward2.

Total Benefit: The CCPC receives $2,220,000 in immediate refundable cash credits ($2,100,000 + $120,000) plus $180,000 in non-refundable ITCs available for 3-year carryback or 20-year carryforward2. (For an ECPC or a non-qualifying CCPC, the $300,000 ITC above the $6,000,000 limit is 0% refundable, yielding $2,100,000 in cash and $300,000 in non-refundable ITCs2.)

body.text: Scenario 2: Federal + Provincial (British Columbia 10%) Stacking Calculation
Consider a qualifying CCPC in British Columbia with $1,000,000 in qualified SR&ED expenditures in 202613:

items: BC Provincial SR&ED Credit (Form T666 — 10% Refundable): $1,000,000 × 10% = $100,000 refundable provincial tax credit13.
Net Federal Qualified Expenditure Pool After Provincial Credit Grind (Line 513): $1,000,000 − $100,000 = $900,00031.
Federal Enhanced SR&ED Credit (Schedule T2SCH31 — 35% Refundable): $900,000 × 35% = $315,000 refundable federal ITC2.
Combined Federal-Provincial Cash Benefit: $100,000 (BC) + $315,000 (Federal) = $415,000 (41.5% of qualified expenditures)37.

body.text: Scenario 3: Proxy Method Calculation with Arm's Length Contract and Materials

Consider a qualifying CCPC in 2026 that incurs $400,000 in directly engaged non-specified employee SR&ED salaries, $30,000 in materials consumed, and $100,000 in an arm's length SR&ED subcontractor payment4:

items: Allowable Section 37 Pool Additions: $400,000 (wages) + $30,000 (materials) + $100,000 (100% of arm's length contract) = $530,00031.
55% Prescribed Proxy Amount (PPA) for ITC Purposes: $400,000 (salary base) × 55% = $220,0004.
80% Inclusion on Arm's Length Contract for ITC Purposes: $100,000 × 80% = $80,00024.
Total Qualified SR&ED Expenditures (Line 570): $400,000 (wages) + $220,000 (PPA) + $30,000 (materials) + $80,000 (80% contract) = $730,00031.
Federal 35% Refundable ITC: $730,000 × 35% = $255,500 cash refund2.

body.text: 5.1 Québec: The 2025–2026 Overhaul — CRIC and CDAEIA

In its March 25, 2025 Budget (Quebec Finance Bulletin 2025-6), the Government of Québec replaced its former R&D salary credit and seven related R&D tax credits for taxation years (or partnership fiscal periods) beginning after March 25, 2025 with the unified Tax Credit for Research, Innovation and Commercialization (CRIC — Crédit d'impôt pour la R-D et la précommercialisation)8. Administered by Revenu Québec, the CRIC is available to any eligible corporation that operates a business in Québec, maintains an establishment there, and undertakes (or causes to be undertaken on its behalf under a contract) eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities in Québec8.

The CRIC provides a 100% refundable tax credit equal to 30% on the first $1,000,000 of qualified expenditures above the applicable exclusion threshold, and 20% on all qualified expenditures exceeding the $1,000,000 threshold8. While Québec legislation remains harmonized with federal legislation regarding the definition of R&D (basic research, applied research, and experimental development) and the CRA continues to carry out the scientific review of R&D work, the CRIC newly covers eligible pre-commercialization activities undertaken in conjunction with R&D work carried out in Québec by or on behalf of the corporation8. Eligible pre-commercialization activities consist of: tests, technological validations, and studies carried out to meet regulatory requirements aimed at obtaining an initial approval or certification to commercialize an innovation (including implementing a quality control system strictly required for initial approval or certification); and product design, including the development of form and aesthetics, improved functionality, and choice of materials8.

Qualified expenditures under the CRIC (reduced by any government or non-government financial assistance) comprise four categories: 100% of salaries or wages paid to the corporation's employees; 50% of amounts paid to a subcontractor for a contract carried out in Québec; 50% of payments made to an eligible public research centre, eligible research consortium, or eligible university entity; and 100% of property acquisition costs (capital property) used in R&D or pre-commercialization in Québec, excluding costs relating to the acquisition of land, a building, or a right to use land or a building8. A corporation cannot stack the CRIC with another Québec tax credit (such as the C3i tax credit for investment and innovation) on the same expenditure, nor claim property used in a large investment project tax holiday8. Before calculating the credit, qualified expenditures must exceed an annual applicable exclusion threshold equal to the greater of $50,000 or the sum of the basic personal amount of the applicable personal income tax system for each employee (adjusted for the percentage of time spent by each employee on eligible R&D or pre-commercialization activities)8. Corporations claim the CRIC by filing Revenu Québec Form RD-1029.8.CR-T (supported where applicable by Form RD-1029.8.EN-T to allocate the $1,000,000 limit among associated corporations and Form RD-1029.8.PR-T for pre-commercialization information)8.

Concurrently, for taxation years beginning after December 31, 2025 (with an early application option in 2025), Québec transitioned its Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business (CDAE)—which previously offered a 30% credit (24% refundable / 6% non-refundable) capped at $83,333 of eligible salary per employee—into the Tax Credit for the Development of E-Business – Innovation and Automation (CDAEIA)10. Under CDAEIA, projects must integrate substantial Artificial Intelligence (AI) or automation that centrally transforms the nature, efficiency, decision-making, or value of the IT product or service (Including data processing and cloud hosting activities, while maintaining revenue tests requiring at least 75% of revenue from IT services and 50% from software development, data processing, or hosting)10. CDAEIA eliminates the $83,333 salary ceiling, introduces a per-employee minimum exclusion threshold ($18,571 in 2025), reduces credit rates by 50% for foreign subsidiaries/dependency links, and gradually shifts the 30% credit split from 23% refundable / 7% non-refundable in 2025 to 22% refundable / 8% non-refundable in 2026, 21% refundable / 9% non-refundable in 2027, and 20% refundable / 10% non-refundable in 202810.
5.2 Ontario: OITC, ORDTC, and OBRITC

Corporations with a permanent establishment in Ontario that are not exempt from corporate income tax under Part III of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) can access three distinct provincial R&D tax credits administered by the CRA69:

items: Ontario Innovation Tax Credit (OITC — Section 96 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)): Provides an 8% refundable tax credit on qualified Ontario SR&ED expenditures (including 100% of current expenditures and eligible repayments) up to an annual expenditure limit of $3,000,000 (shared among associated corporations, yielding up to $240,000 in annual cash refunds)77. The $3,000,000 expenditure limit begins to reduce when the combined previous-year federal taxable income of the corporation and its associated corporations exceeds $500,000 (becoming nil at $800,000), or when the combined previous-year specified capital amount reaches $25,000,000 (becoming nil at $50,000,000)77. Claimed on Schedule 566 (Ontario Innovation Tax Credit, requiring Form T661 and Schedule 31) and entered on Line 468 of Schedule 5; may be waived in whole or in part under subsection 96(14)77.

Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit (ORDTC — Sections 38 to 45 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)): Provides a 3.5% non-refundable tax credit (reduced from 4.5% for tax years ending on or after June 1, 2016) on eligible Ontario SR&ED expenditures (reduced by government assistance, including any OITC or OBRITC), with no expenditure cap69. Unused ORDTC carries back 3 taxation years and carries forward 20 taxation years69. Claimed on Schedule 508 (Ontario Research and Development Tax Credit) and entered on Line 416 of Schedule 5 (with recapture under section 45 reported on Line 277 of Schedule 5)69. A corporation may waive the current-year ORDTC in whole or in part under subsection 43(1) of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario) so that the non-refundable credit does not reduce its 35% refundable federal SR&ED expenditure pool69.

Ontario Business-Research Institute Tax Credit (OBRITC — Section 97 of the Taxation Act, 2007 (Ontario)): Provides a 20% refundable tax credit on qualified expenditures incurred in Ontario under an eligible contract with an Eligible Research Institute (ERI) (Ontario universities, colleges of applied arts and technology, hospital research institutes, Ontario Centres of Excellence, and Networks of Centres of Excellence) up to an annual qualified expenditure limit of $20,000,000 per associated group ($4,000,000 maximum annual credit)78. Claimed on Schedule 568 and Schedule 569 (reporting the ERI Code for each contract) and entered on Line 470 of Schedule 578.

body.text: 5.3 British Columbia: Permanent BC SR&ED Tax Credit

Under Part 6 of the British Columbia Income Tax Act, the British Columbia SR&ED Tax Credit is now permanent13. Qualifying CCPCs and—for taxation years starting after December 15, 2024—qualifying Eligible Canadian Public Corporations (ECPCs) with a permanent establishment in BC earn a 10% refundable tax credit equal to 10% of the lesser of their SR&ED qualified BC expenditure for the year and their expenditure limit (entered on Line 674 of Schedule 5)13. Qualifying CCPCs and ECPCs with BC SR&ED expenditures exceeding their expenditure limit, as well as other qualifying corporations (and active corporate members of a partnership), earn a 10% non-refundable credit on excess BC expenditures (entered on Line 659 of Schedule 5; carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years; renunciation permitted under subsection 100(1) of the BC Income Tax Act)13. Claimed on Form T666 (British Columbia (BC) Scientific Research and Experimental Development Tax Credit), which must be filed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year; BC recapture within 10 years of acquisition under sections 102.1 to 102.6 is reported on Line 241 of Schedule 513.
5.4 Alberta: Innovation Employment Grant (IEG)

Administered by the Alberta Tax and Revenue Administration (TRA) (launched March 29, 2021 to replace the former Alberta SR&ED credit), the Alberta Innovation Employment Grant (IEG) is a refundable tax credit for small and medium-sized corporations with a permanent establishment in Alberta75. The IEG provides an 8% base credit on the corporation's base level of Alberta R&D spending (calculated as the corporation's average qualifying Alberta R&D expenditures over the previous 2 taxation years) plus an enhanced 20% credit (8% base + 12% incremental) on qualifying Alberta R&D spending that exceeds that two-year base level, up to $4,000,000 in annual R&D spending75. The $4,000,000 maximum expenditure limit phases out incrementally when the prior-year taxable capital employed in Canada of the corporation and its associated group is between $10,000,000 and $50,000,000, reaching nil at $50,000,00075. Claimed on the Alberta corporate return using AT1 Schedule 29 (Form AT29) and Form AT4970 (Listing of SR&ED Projects Carried Out in Alberta)75.
5.5 Prairie Provinces: Saskatchewan and Manitoba

Under the Saskatchewan Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule 403), corporations with a permanent establishment in Saskatchewan earn a 10% tax credit on eligible Saskatchewan SR&ED expenditures (plus repayments of government assistance)9. For taxation years beginning after December 15, 2024, CCPCs earn a 10% refundable credit on the first $2,000,000 of eligible expenditures—doubled from the $1,000,000 refundable limit that applied to taxation years beginning before December 16, 2024 (Line 645 of Schedule 5)9. Expenditures above the $2,000,000 CCPC limit, and all expenditures by non-CCPCs, earn a 10% non-refundable credit (Line 631 of Schedule 5; carryback 3 years, carryforward 10 years; renunciation permitted under subsection 63.4(13) of the Saskatchewan Income Tax Act, 2000), subject to a combined annual maximum credit cap of $1,000,000 for refundable and non-refundable credits combined9.

Under the Manitoba Research and Development Tax Credit (Schedule 380), corporations with a permanent establishment in Manitoba earn a 15% tax credit on eligible Manitoba R&D expenditures (including current expenditures, capital expenditures for depreciable property excluding buildings or leasehold interests in buildings, First and Second Term SUE, and repayments of government assistance)71. When the R&D is carried out in Manitoba under an eligible contract with a qualifying research institute, 100% of the 15% credit is refundable; otherwise, 50% of the credit is refundable (Line 613 of Schedule 5) and 50% is non-refundable (Line 606 of Schedule 5; carryback 3 years, carryforward 20 years; renunciation available under subsection 7.3(7) of the Income Tax Act (Manitoba))71. Eligible expenditures must be identified on Schedule 380 no later than 12 months after the T2 return due date71.
5.6 Atlantic Provinces and Territories: Nova Scotia, New Brunswick, Newfoundland and Labrador, and Yukon

All three Atlantic provinces offering R&D tax credits, as well as the Yukon Territory, provide 15% fully refundable tax credits (applied first against total taxes payable) with no upper expenditure limit70:

items: Nova Scotia (Schedule 340): 15% fully refundable credit on eligible Nova Scotia R&D expenditures (Line 566 of Schedule 5), filed no later than 18 months after the corporation's tax year-end; renunciation available under subsection 41(7) of the Income Tax Act (Nova Scotia); recapture reported on Line 221 of Schedule 570.
New Brunswick (Schedule 360): 15% fully refundable credit on eligible New Brunswick R&D expenditures (Line 597 of Schedule 5), with recapture reported on Line 573 of Schedule 574.

Newfoundland and Labrador (Schedule 301): 15% fully refundable credit on eligible Newfoundland and Labrador R&D expenditures (Line 520 of Schedule 5), filed no later than 12 months after the corporation's T2 filing due date73.

Yukon Territory (Schedule 442): 15% fully refundable base credit on eligible Yukon R&D expenditures plus an additional 5% fully refundable bonus credit (totalling 20% refundable) on eligible expenditures paid or payable to Yukon University (Line 698 of Schedule 5), filed no later than 18 months after the end of the taxation year72.

6.1 Governing Authorities and Administrative Structure

Governance of the federal SR&ED program is shared between the Department of Finance Canada, which formulates tax legislation and explanatory notes under the Income Tax Act and Income Tax Regulations (and approves prescribed special-purpose buildings), and the Canada Revenue Agency (CRA) — SR&ED Directorate, which administers the program, publishes binding administrative policies and guidelines, processes tax returns, and conducts technical and financial reviews16. Within the CRA, claim reviews are executed jointly by Research and Technology Advisors (RTAs)—who evaluate whether the claimed projects meet the scientific and technological eligibility requirements of subsection 248(1) (occasionally assisted by external Outside Consultants (OCs))—and Financial Reviewers (FRs), who audit the supporting financial ledgers, salary caps, proxy calculations, unpaid amounts, and assistance reductions7.
