Across its 10 parts, the updated 2026 Form T661 captures the following line-by-line information5:

items: Part 1 – General Information (Lines 010 to 157): Captures the registered business or partnership name (Line 010), 15-character Business Number (BN), taxation year start and end dates, total number of SR&ED projects claimed (Line 050), financial contact person (Lines 100–110), technical contact person (Lines 115–125), and partnership details (Lines 151–157)31.

Part 2 – Project Information (Completed on a Project-by-Project Basis): Section A records the project title and code (Line 200), start date (Line 202), completion or expected completion date (Line 204), Field of Science or Technology code and new Canada Research and Development Classification (CRDC) field-of-research code (Line 206), Pre-Claim Approval case number (added for 2026), continuation claim history (Lines 208–210), and collaborative partners (Lines 218–221)5. Section B contains the three mandatory technical narrative questions (subject to strict word limits on the form): Line 242 ("What technological obstacles/uncertainties did you overcome to achieve the technological advancements described in Line 240?"), Line 244 ("What work did you perform in the tax year to overcome the technological obstacles/uncertainties described in Line 242?"), and Line 246 ("What scientific or technological advancements did you achieve as a result of the work described in Line 244?")31. Section C identifies who drafted Section B (Lines 253–259), key directly involved employees and external consultants (Lines 260–261), the names of the 10 most expensive SR&ED capital properties acquired after December 15, 2024 used in each project (Lines 262–263), work performed outside Canada (Line 265), work carried out on behalf of another party (Line 266), and non-employee involvement (Lines 267–269), while Section D (Lines 270–282) records project planning documents and contemporaneous supporting evidence31.

Part 3 – Calculation of SR&ED Expenditures (Lines 160 to 470): Section A records the irrevocable election of the Proxy Method (Line 160) or Traditional Method (Line 162)5. Section B calculates allowable SR&ED expenditures: Canadian salaries/wages for non-specified employees (Line 300) and specified employees (Line 305); permissible foreign salaries/wages (up to 10%) for non-specified employees (Line 307) and specified employees (Line 309); prior-year unpaid wages paid in the year (Line 310); less current-year wages unpaid after 180 days (Line 315); materials consumed (Line 320); materials transformed (Line 325); arm's length SR&ED contracts (Line 340); non-arm's length SR&ED contracts (Line 345); equipment lease costs incurred after December 15, 2024; overhead and other expenditures under the Traditional Method (Line 360); third-party payments per Form T1263 (Line 370); total current SR&ED expenditures (Line 380); restored SR&ED capital expenditures for depreciable property acquired after December 15, 2024 (Line 390); and Total Allowable SR&ED Expenditures (Line 400)31. Section C calculates the Section 37 Pool of Deductible SR&ED Expenditures by subtracting provincial, other government, and non-government assistance (Lines 429–432), prior-year SR&ED ITCs applied or refunded (Line 435), and CCA recapture adjustments (Line 440) to determine the available deduction and closing pool carryforward (Lines 440–470)31.

body.text: 6.3 Statutory Filing Deadlines: The Strict 18-Month Rule

Under subsection 37(11) (for deducting expenditures) and paragraph (m) of the definition of "investment tax credit" in subsection 127(9) (for earning ITCs), a claimant's SR&ED reporting deadline is 12 months after the filing due date of the income tax return for the taxation year in which the expenditures were incurred19. Because a corporation's T2 return is due 6 months after its taxation year-end under paragraph 150(1)(a), a corporation's SR&ED reporting deadline is 18 months after its taxation year-end (for example, if the tax year ends on the last day of a month such as February 28, the T2 is due August 31 and the SR&ED reporting deadline is August 31 of the following year; if the tax year ends on January 6, the T2 is due July 6 and the SR&ED reporting deadline is July 6 of the following year)20. For an individual carrying on an unincorporated business, the T1 return is due June 15, making the SR&ED reporting deadline June 15 of the following year19.

There is no statutory mechanism to extend the SR&ED reporting deadline22. If Form T661 containing the prescribed information is filed after the 18-month reporting deadline, no SR&ED expenditures or ITCs are allowed7. If Form T661 is filed on time but Schedule T2SCH31 or Form T2038(IND) is filed after the reporting deadline, the claimant may deduct the allowable expenditures in the Section 37 pool, but forfeits all ITCs for that year20. If a claim is filed at least 90 days before the reporting deadline, the CRA has sufficient time to perform an initial review and advise the claimant of any deficiencies before the deadline expires20. Separately, Form T1145 (NAL assistance allocation) must be filed on or before the transferor's income tax return filing due date for the year, or within the period in which the transferor or transferee may serve a Notice of Objection under Part I20.
6.4 The Optional Pre-Claim Approval Process (Launched April 1, 2026 — Form T1322)

Effective April 1, 2026, the CRA launched an optional SR&ED Pre-Claim Approval process allowing eligible businesses to obtain an upfront determination within 8 weeks on whether their planned projects meet the definition of SR&ED under subsection 248(1) before starting work or incurring significant costs1. To qualify, the business must operate in Canada as a CCPC, other Canadian corporation, or partnership, have annual gross business income of less than $25,000,000, and be in good standing with the CRA, while the planned project (up to a maximum of 3 projects per application) must not have been included in a previous SR&ED claim and must not involve issues currently under objection or in litigation42.
The application follows a structured four-step workflow42:

items: Request a Case Number: The business submits an eligibility request on Canada.ca; existing SR&ED claimants receive a case number in My Business Account within 2 business days, while new claimants receive a phone call from the CRA within 5 business days42.

Complete Form T1322 (Section B Word Limits): The applicant completes Form T1322 (Application for Scientific Research and Experimental Development (SR&ED) pre-claim approval), including Part 1 identification (Lines 010–016) and Part 2 project details (Lines 020–032)43. Section B of Form T1322 requires three narrative responses per project with strict word limits: Line 042 (Maximum 500 words) asking "What scientific or technological uncertainty do you aim to address?"; Line 043 (Maximum 700 words) asking "What due diligence have you completed to confirm that the scientific or technical uncertainty described in line 042 cannot be resolved using existing knowledge, solutions or approaches?"; and Line 044 (Maximum 900 words) asking "What work do you plan to perform, during the pre-claim approval period (up to 3 years), to overcome the scientific or technological uncertainty described at line 042? Describe the hypotheses, proposed solutions or approaches to be tested by experiment or analysis."43

Upload Supporting Documents (Section D) via My Business Account: The applicant uploads project planning documents (Gantt charts, work breakdown structures, schedules), a description of planned internal controls for tracking SR&ED time, expenses, and contemporaneous records, due diligence technical references/diagrams, and a list of project team members with their credentials and expertise43.

RTA Meeting, 8-Week Written Decision, 3-Year Validity, and 90-Day Expenditure Review: An assigned RTA conducts a 2-to-5-hour virtual or on-site meeting (mandatory for new claimants; optional for existing claimants in good standing) and issues a written Pre-Claim Approval Evaluation Report within 8 weeks of receiving the complete application42. If approved, the pre-claim approval is valid for up to 3 years, and when the claimant subsequently files its annual Form T661, claims containing only pre-approved projects that are selected for an expenditure review have their processing time cut in half from 180 days to 90 days1.

For refundable SR&ED claims (there are no published service standards for non-refundable claims, which are assessed as filed and audited prior to the normal statute-barred reassessment date), the CRA's published processing service standards from the date a complete claim and income tax return are received are: within 60 calendar days for claims accepted as filed (with an internal 45-day target noted by industry sources from April 2026 for timely non-reviewed claims); within 90 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review that only include projects granted Pre-Claim Approval; and within 180 calendar days for refundable claims selected for review that include any project not granted Pre-Claim Approval or materially differing from a pre-approved project7.

According to the CRA's Annual Program Statistics (updated April 30, 2026), the SR&ED program delivered $4.6 billion in allowed ITCs across 23,677 processed claims in the fiscal year ended March 31, 2026—with 90% of claims accepted as filed, 6% accepted after modifications, and 4% denied1. body.text: First-time claimants (or businesses that have not filed an SR&ED claim in the past 3 years) may be selected for the mandatory First-Time Claimant Advisory Service (FTCAS), which provides educational recommendations to support future compliance7. When a claim is selected for technical and financial review (governed by The SR&ED Review Process: A Guide for Claimants and the CRA's Financial Claim Review Manual), the RTA and FR establish a Review Plan, conduct an initial interview and site or virtual visit with technical and financial personnel, evaluate contemporaneous records (watching for common audit deficiencies such as estimated costs with little or no rationale, unreliable documentation created months after the SR&ED was performed, double-counting of costs, and improper year-end cutoff), and issue a draft Proposal Letter and Summary of Adjustments before finalizing the Financial Review Report (FRR)7.

If a claimant has concerns during a review, they should first speak to the RTA and/or FR, and if unresolved, escalate to the Research and Technology Manager and/or Financial Review Manager (using Form RC532, Request for Administrative Review)7. Once a Notice of Assessment or Reassessment is sent, a corporate taxpayer has 90 days under paragraph 165(1)(b) of the ITA to serve a formal Notice of Objection7. Under subsections 166.1(7) and 166.2(5), an application for an extension of time to object can only be granted if made within 1 year after the expiration of the initial 90-day period (a strict outer limit of 1 year and 90 days from the mailing date of the Notice of Assessment), after which the taxpayer may appeal an adverse decision to the Tax Court of Canada7.
7. Landmark Canadian Jurisprudence and Audit Precedents

Canadian SR&ED law is heavily shaped by judicial precedents from the Tax Court of Canada (TCC) and the Federal Court of Appeal (FCA)63. Any rigorous technical narrative or audit defence must align with the following binding cases.
7.1 The Foundational Five-Question Test: Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 TCC), RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 FCA), and C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada (2001 FCA)

In Northwest Hydraulic Consultants Ltd. v. The Queen, 98 DTC 1839, 1998 CanLII 553 (TCC), Justice Donald Bowman articulated the foundational five-criterion legal test for determining whether an activity constitutes SR&ED under subsection 248(1) of the ITA52. This five-step framework was expressly endorsed by the Federal Court of Appeal in RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen, 99 DTC 5087, 235 N.R. 258 (FCA 1998) and summarized into five canonical questions by the Federal Court of Appeal in C.W. Agencies Inc. v. Canada, 2001 FCA 393, 2002 DTC 6740 (FCA)50:

items: Question 1 (Technological Risk or Uncertainty): Was there a technological risk or uncertainty which could not be removed by routine engineering or standard procedures?50 Justice Bowman defined "routine engineering" as techniques, procedures, and data that are generally accessible to competent professionals in the field52. If the problem can be resolved by applying known engineering principles or standard procedures, there is no technological uncertainty52.

Question 2 (Formulation of Hypotheses): Did the person claiming to be doing SR&ED formulate hypotheses specifically aimed at reducing or eliminating that technological uncertainty?50 In Northwest Hydraulic, Justice Bowman held that this involves a five-stage process: observation of the subject matter of the problem; formulation of a clear objective; identification and articulation of the technological uncertainty; formulation of a hypothesis or hypotheses designed to reduce or eliminate the uncertainty; and methodical and systematic testing of the hypotheses51.

Question 3 (Accordance with the Scientific Method): Did the procedures adopted accord with the total discipline of the scientific method, including the formulation, testing, and modification of hypotheses?50 The procedures must be characterized by trained and systematic observation, measurement, and experiment, rather than routine trial and error50.

Question 4 (Technological Advancement): Did the process result in a technological advancement, that is to say, an advancement in the general understanding?50 Justice Bowman clarified two vital principles under Question 4: first, "general understanding" means something that is known to, or available to, persons knowledgeable in the field (not a piece of knowledge that may be known to someone somewhere); and second, the rejection after testing of a hypothesis is nonetheless an advance in that it eliminates one hitherto untested hypothesis, and failure to achieve the initial objective reinforces the measure of the technological uncertainty52.
Question 5 (Contemporaneous Detailed Records): Was a detailed record of the hypotheses, tests, and results kept as the work progressed?50

body.text: In RIS-Christie Ltd. v. The Queen (1998 FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal reinforced that the statute requires research to be undertaken for the purpose of achieving technological advancement, not that it actually culminate in a successful product ("Presumably, not all of Alexander Graham Bell's research initiatives bore fruit. To maintain that failed research efforts do not constitute scientific research under the Act is contrary to common sense and the goal of encouraging entrepreneurship")55. Furthermore, on Question 5 (documentation), the Federal Court of Appeal held in RIS-Christie that while documentary evidence is "the only sure-fire way" of establishing that systematic scientific research was undertaken, if a taxpayer has a plausible explanation for the failure to adduce documentary evidence of repeatability data and establishes through credible oral (viva voce) and expert testimony that testing was undertaken and achieved a technological advancement, the court will not impose an additional evidentiary burden that precludes oral evidence50.

7.2 Scientific Method and Routine Engineering: Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA), Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen (2017 TCC 6), National R&D Inc. v. The Queen (2020 TCC 47), and Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen (2021 FCA 88)

Subsequent appellate and trial decisions have strictly policed the boundary between systematic scientific investigation and undocumented "trial and error" or routine engineering. In Jentel Manufacturing Ltd. v. The Queen (2011 FCA), the Federal Court of Appeal reaffirmed the mandatory application of the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria to SR&ED claims63. In Joel Theatrical Rigging Contractors (1980) Ltd. v. The Queen, 2017 TCC 6, the taxpayer designed and installed theatrical rigging and claimed two projects: a motorized fire curtain descent control system without counterweights (2008) and a manual override system for a curtain machine (2009)97. Dismissing the appeal, the Tax Court of Canada noted that neither the company's president nor the external SR&ED consultant who drafted Form T661 held a university degree in mechanical engineering or a Professional Engineer (P.Eng.) designation, none of the company's designers with engineering training testified at the hearing, and the company did not consult a professional engineer during the experimentation97. Consequently, the taxpayer failed to discharge its burden of proving that the work was not routine engineering92.

Similarly, in National R&D Inc. v. The Queen, 2020 TCC 47—which involved the development of a computer program to automate portions of filing SR&ED claims—the Tax Court confirmed that software development claims must adhere to the scientific method through formal hypothesis formulation and systematic experimental verification54. In Kam-Press Metal Products Ltd. v. The Queen, 2021 FCA 88 (affirming 2019 TCC 246), the appellant metal-stamping manufacturer argued before the Federal Court of Appeal that because there is no reference to "scientific method" in the statutory text of subsection 248(1) of the ITA, the Tax Court Judge erred in applying Justice Bowman's third criterion from Northwest Hydraulic93. Writing for a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal, Justice Webb dismissed the appeal, holding that Justice Bowman was interpreting the statutory definition of SR&ED in subsection 248(1) and that the five Northwest Hydraulic criteria—repeatedly endorsed by the FCA in RIS-Christie, C.W. Agencies, and Jentel Manufacturing—remain binding law93.
7.3 Modern Jurisprudence on Context, Economic Constraints, Government Assistance, and Procedural Limitation Periods (2021–2025)

Recent rulings between 2021 and late 2025 have clarified several nuanced areas of SR&ED audit defence. In 6398316 Canada Inc. v. The Queen, 2021 TCC 17 (concerning construction expenses for a house completed in late 2013), Justice Lafleur held that "business constraints and the business context of the taxpayer that is claiming the SR&ED deduction and credit are relevant factors to take into account when considering the criterion of technological uncertainty", while cautioning that taxpayers must frame their hypothesis and technological uncertainty to highlight technological rather than purely economic obstacles54.

In CAE Inc. v. His Majesty the King, 2022 FCA 178 (affirming 2021 TCC 57), CAE Inc. entered into a March 30, 2009 agreement with Industry Canada for "Project Falcon" under the Strategic Aerospace and Defence Initiative, receiving repayable financial contributions in 2012 and 201363. Both the Tax Court (per Ouimet J.) and a unanimous Federal Court of Appeal (per Boivin J.A.) held that because the implicit rate of return on the loan was significantly lower than the market rate of return for a comparable loan from a private lender, the funds were not paid under an ordinary business agreement and constituted "government assistance" under subsection 127(9)—reducing CAE's SR&ED ITCs and requiring income inclusion63. The FCA rejected CAE's argument that a legal distinction should be drawn between the capital loan principal and the interest rate differential63.

In Canafric Inc. v. The King (2023 TCC), a food manufacturer producing custom frozen pies for major retailers appealed the CRA's denial of $343,449 in SR&ED expenditures ($60,963 in ITCs) across projects from 2013 to 2016 involving salt/fat reduction, shelf-life extension without preservatives, and maintaining structural integrity after freezing50. Allowing the appeal on six projects, Justice Bodie held that: (1) a technological uncertainty can be established even where known ingredients or solutions exist, provided no public or scientific information existed on how to combine them in the specific context; (2) Canafric did not merely use routine trial and error by discarding failed recipes, but systematically analyzed why each recipe failed and adjusted parameters based on observation and measurement in accordance with the scientific method; and (3) citing RIS-Christie, clear, factually grounded oral testimony from Canafric's CEO successfully filled gaps in the written documentation to satisfy Question 550.

Finally, in Simon Ribbans Photography Inc. v. The King, 2025 TCC 146 (decided October 14, 2025), the taxpayer applied under subsection 166.2(1) of the ITA for an extension of time to file a Notice of Objection to Notices of Assessment dated September 13, 2022, asserting it never received the notices until Fall 2023 and serving its objection on January 18, 202463. Applying the four-step evidentiary framework under subsections 244(10), 244(14), 244(15), and 248(7)(a), Justice Sylvain Ouimet accepted the CRA's Print-to-Mail and IQ tracking system affidavits establishing that the notices were printed and delivered to Canada Post on September 13, 202263. Once mailing is established, paragraph 248(7)(a) creates an irrebuttable presumption of receipt on the mailing date63. Because the January 18, 2024 objection was served after the mandatory 1-year-and-90-day statutory deadline of December 12, 2023, the Tax Court held it had no legal jurisdiction under subsection 166.2(5) to grant an extension63.
